title: The Entropic Dimensional Framework – V2 – Projection-Induced Geometry, Gauge Structure, and Regularization
content: The Entropic Dimensional Framework (EDF) pursues a structural approach based on a finite and convergent dynamics aimed to avoid singularities, UV divergences and open issues in quantum and relativistic Physics. The EDF version 1 [1] introduced a global-to-local perspective where entropy and information are formalized by four functorial projections \(P_n\) (\(n = 0, 1, 2, 3\)) with non-trivial kernels. This EDF version 2 stands on the same perspective, and reinforces the structural character of the hypothesis. Here, a projection hierarchy acts on information-bearing quantum structures, while a finite phase resolver and primitive cyclic traversal generate the complete matrix algebra \(M_k(\mathbb{C})\) with closure capacity \(C(k) = k^2\). An independent Fibonacci compatibility condition selects the nontrivial finite closure \(k = 12\), with \(\mathbb{Z}_{12} \cong \mathbb{Z}_3 \times \mathbb{Z}_4\). Starting from this established finite structure, the present work derives consequences that were not assumed in the original construction. A smoothly parameterized EDF projector \(P(x)\) is shown to generate both a gauge-invariant quantum metric and a non-Abelian connection curvature. Thus geometry and gauge structure arise from a common projection object rather than being introduced as independent postulates. Bounds on derivatives of \(P\) directly bound the induced metric and gauge curvature, providing a precise projection-regularity criterion for the avoidance of local geometric divergences. The same projection architecture is then extended to a cumulative momentum-transfer kernel, from which regularized sources, ultraviolet suppression, and a scale-dependent spectral dimension are developed. The entropy hierarchy is further promoted to quantum channels through monotonicity of relative entropy, allowing projected information loss and recoverability to be related to the residual-memory structure of EDF. Finally, the induced connection permits the finite braid sector to be formulated as a holonomy problem, while the \(\mathbb{Z}_3\) factor gives a constrained three-sector spectral operator. The resulting construction does not identify these mathematical structures with particular interactions by assumption. Rather, it shows that a single finite projection architecture is sufficient to generate geometry, connection, regularization, information descent, and finite-sector topology, thereby defining concrete physical and experimental discriminators for the framework.
